Changes in Marriage Incidence in Western Society 127 more than doubled; and at 25–29 the rate is up by nearly half as much again. The relatively greater increases in marriage rates at younger ages reflects a tendency of modern spinsters to marry earlier in life than their predecessors. The mean age at marriage of spinsters has fallen from 25.47 years in 1931 to 23.37. The average age of spinsters marrying bachelors in 1959 was 22.6 years, 2.6 years younger, on average, than their husbands. A quarter of all spinster brides in 1959 were under 20 years of age compared with 10% in 1931.

4. THE SOCIAL AND ECONOMIC BACKGROUND There are a number of factors which have operated to bring about these changes. In Britain, and in the Western world generally, the last thirty years have been marked by great social advances. After the economic depression of the early thirties steps were taken in most countries to eliminate poverty in its most severe degree and to intro duce measures of social security. In the mood of reconstruction after World War II this movement was accelerated. In Britain especially, the term ‘Welfare State’ acquired a real significance. In addition there has been a prolonged period of full employment, first to prepare for war, later to recover from it as well as to participate in the accelerated world economic development of the post-war years. This has affected the situation in two ways. First there is a very sharp contrast between C

able to contemplate marriage against a background of joint earnings and a 
high level of living from the outset. Marriage need not, as was formerly 
the case, be deferred until savings have been acquired to furnish a home 
and provide a bulwark against any risk of economic troubles in the 
early years of marriage. It is not the purpose of this paper to discuss 
the normality or otherwise of teen-age marriage but at least it may be 
stressed that there is no longer any economic obstacle to early marriage. 
Another factor to be mentioned is the general emancipation of women. 
Marriage is no longer regarded as the only ‘safe’ career for a girl. 
Socially, as well as economically, girls can regard marriage as incidental 
to their fuller lives. This is not to suggest that they take marriage 
lightly. On the contrary it is the author’s personal view that the young 
married couples of today, on the whole, take if anything a more re 
sponsible attitude towards marriage and parenthood than earlier genera 
tions—certainly no less. But as regards the timing of marriage, girls 
do not regard themselves as waiting to be ‘married off’ after a respec 
table period of courtship. 
For completeness, though this is the subject of another paper, it should 
be made clear that the precipitation of marriage by pregnancy is not a 
primary factor in the lowering of marriage age. Each year in England 
and Wales there are about 100,000 maternities resulting from extra 
marital conception, and about 60% of these are legitimated by the 
marriage of the parents before the birth of the child, But there were 
just as many such maternities thirty years ago (when the general level 
of fertility was much lower) and a somewhat higher proportion (70%) 
were legitimated by marriage.
